nameStory: The waterwheel plant gets its delightful name from the way its tiny traps are arranged in perfect circles around its floating stem, just like the paddles on an old-fashioned waterwheel. Each whorl of traps spins around the central stem as the plant drifts through the water, creating a living, hunting waterwheel that's constantly ready to snap shut on unsuspecting prey.
description: The waterwheel plant is an extraordinary floating carnivorous plant that lives entirely underwater in ponds and slow streams. This remarkable hunter drifts freely through the water with no roots, using dozens of tiny snap-traps arranged in wheel-like clusters around its thin, thread-like stem. The whole plant is typically only 4-6 inches long, but it's one of the world's most active carnivorous plants, capable of lightning-fast movements to catch small water creatures.

idTips.label: Traps
idTips.description: Tiny hinged traps arranged in perfect whorls around the stem, each about the size of a pinky nail and shaped like miniature clamshells that can snap shut in milliseconds when touched

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Completely free-floating with no roots whatsoever, drifting just below the water surface like a delicate green necklace

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Thread-thin central stem that feels smooth and slightly rubbery, often appearing segmented where each whorl of traps emerges

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: What look like leaves are actually modified trap structures with fine, hair-like projections that wave gently in the current

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Traps visibly snap shut when disturbed, moving faster than you can blink - one of the few plants you can actually watch move

habitat: Found in very clean, nutrient-poor ponds, slow-moving streams, and bog pools with soft, acidic water. In New England, it appears in pristine wetlands and some artificial ponds, always in still or barely moving water with excellent water quality. It requires full sun and cannot tolerate polluted or nutrient-rich water.

seasonality.spring: Plants emerge from winter dormancy as small growing tips, quickly developing their first whorls of active traps as water temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with fully developed trap wheels actively hunting, and tiny white flowers may appear at the water surface on rare occasions.
seasonality.fall: Plants form winter dormancy buds and begin to sink deeper in the water as traps become less active with cooling temperatures.
seasonality.winter: Survives as small dormant buds resting in the sediment or suspended deep in the water column, completely inactive until spring warmth returns.

funFact: The waterwheel plant is basically an underwater Venus flytrap that can snap its traps shut in just 1/10th of a second - so fast that it creates tiny water currents that actually help suck prey into its mouth-like traps!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with submerged aquatic weeds like hornwort or water milfoil, but those have feathery leaves that don't move and lack the distinctive snap-traps arranged in perfect wheels around the stem.
contextualKnowledge: Though extremely rare with only 50 populations left worldwide, waterwheel plants in New England may actually be from introduced populations rather than native ones, as the species has mysteriously appeared in some locations where it wasn't historically recorded. The plant is popular among carnivorous plant enthusiasts but requires expert care in cultivation.
compareHints: As the only species in its genus Aldrovanda, waterwheel plant is most similar to its famous cousin the Venus flytrap, but differs by being completely aquatic and having its traps arranged in whorls rather than in a ground-hugging rosette. Unlike other plants in the sundew family that use sticky traps, waterwheel plants use mechanical snap-traps just like Venus flytraps.
